walkthroughs.body_html:
Tests for Ions & Gases — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Tests for Ions & Gases brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Tests for Ions & Gases.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A lilac flame test colour indicates which ion?
options: Potassium
Sodium
Calcium
Copper

mcqs.q: The test for carbon dioxide is that it:
options: Turns limewater milky
Pops with a lit splint
Relights a glowing splint
Bleaches damp litmus paper

mcqs.q: Sodium hydroxide solution gives a blue precipitate with a solution containing:
options: Cu²⁺ ions
Fe²⁺ ions
Fe³⁺ ions
Ca²⁺ ions

mcqs.q: Acidified silver nitrate gives a yellow precipitate with:
options: Iodide ions
Chloride ions
Bromide ions
Sulfate ions

mcqs.q: Does the squeaky pop test detect oxygen?
options: No — the pop with a lit splint is the test for hydrogen; oxygen relights a glowing splint instead.
Oxygen gives the squeaky pop because it supports burning.
The squeaky pop test detects carbon dioxide.
Hydrochloric acid is normally used because it makes the test stronger.

mcqs.q: Why is dilute nitric acid added before the silver nitrate halide test?
options: The squeaky pop test detects carbon dioxide.
The acid is there to dissolve the silver halide precipitate so it shows up better.
Hydrochloric acid is normally used because it makes the test stronger.
The acid removes carbonate ions, which would otherwise form a white silver carbonate precipitate and give a false positive.

mcqs.q: Do Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ solutions give the same colour with sodium hydroxide?
options: Hydrochloric acid is normally used because it makes the test stronger.
All iron solutions give the same rusty-brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide.
No — Fe²⁺ gives a green precipitate and Fe³⁺ gives a brown one, which is how the two iron ions are distinguished.
Iron ions give a blue precipitate just like copper ions.
